metadata.description:
Propagation Geometry: Directional Substrate Transmission and the SR Theory of Pathway‑Mediated Receiver Change

DESCRIPTION

Propagation Geometry is a canonical SR subfield of Infrastructure Science that studies directional, carrier‑based transmission of disturbances across multilayer substrate networks. Its irreducible object is:

“directional pathway‑mediated receiver change.”

A propagation event requires a source, trigger, carrier, directed path, receiver, clock discipline, and receiver‑domain change, each explicitly declared. As the manuscript states:

“Propagation is not inferred from correlation, temporal coincidence, shared exposure, synchronized failure, or similar outcomes.”

Propagation Geometry replaces thematic similarity with supported edges, meaning:

  • no edge exists until a carrier is measured

  • no direction exists until clocks align

  • no transformation exists until receiver‑domain mapping is declared

  • no propagation exists until rivals (common shock, independent failure, reverse path) are ruled out

The field defines:

  • supported directional edges (Equation 1)

  • receiver transitions with transformation (Equation 2)

  • path gain and delay (Equation 3)

  • local propagation regimes (Equation 4)

  • blocker effects (Equation 5)

It establishes strict boundaries: drift, collapse, correlation, diffusion, contagion, synchronized outcomes, and causal graphs do not constitute propagation without carrier evidence.

Propagation Geometry is falsifiable. Unsupported edges remain zero. A path is rejected when:

“Receiver change precedes the asserted source,”
“Path interruption does not alter receiver outcomes,”
or common‑shock models perform equally well.”

The field earns standing only when supported pathways improve explanation, prediction, or intervention beyond mature domain models.

HOW IT CONTRIBUTES TO SR

1. It gives SR a formal, falsifiable transmission mechanism

Propagation Geometry is the first SR field that defines how disturbances move through infrastructure, institutions, and multilayer systems.
It replaces narrative causation with:

  • carriers

  • clocks

  • directed edges

  • transformations

  • rivals

  • blockers

  • topology change

Linked concept: Directional Transmission

2. It establishes the substrate‑level geometry for Infrastructure Science

Infrastructure Science needed a field that could explain movement, not just state.
Propagation Geometry provides:

  • multilayer topology

  • carrier identity

  • path gain

  • delay

  • bypass

  • feedback

  • recovery interference

Linked concept: Infrastructure Science

3. It prevents false propagation claims

The manuscript states:

“Unsupported edges remain zero rather than entering a model through thematic similarity.”

This protects SR from:

  • correlation mistaken as transmission

  • synchronized outcomes mistaken as causation

  • narrative similarity mistaken as path

  • domain drift mistaken as propagation

Linked concept: Common Shock Discipline

4. It defines the minimum propagation event record

Propagation Geometry introduces the strictest event record in SR:

  • source

  • trigger

  • carrier

  • path

  • receiver

  • clocks

  • rivals

  • falsifier

This becomes the standard for all SR transmission claims.

Linked concept: Propagation Event Record

5. It introduces transformation discipline

Propagation Geometry is the first SR field to require explicit mapping when the disturbance changes form:

“A source outage can create delay at one receiver and manual work at another without making outage, delay, and work interchangeable quantities.”

This protects SR from category drift and unit confusion.

Linked concept: Receiver Transformation

6. It formalizes blockers and susceptibility

Propagation Geometry defines blockers as causal components, not noise:

  • redundancy

  • segmentation

  • substitution

  • reserve capacity

  • access controls

Receiver susceptibility becomes measurable rather than assumed.

Linked concept: Blocker Effects

7. It introduces recovery interference as a propagation regime

Recovery interference — when a failure disables the systems needed to repair it — becomes a formal propagation regime:

“Recovery action then becomes unavailable or generates a new disturbance.”

This is foundational for SR Collapse Geometry and SR Recovery Architecture.

Linked concept: Recovery Interference

8. It establishes bridges to other SR fields

Propagation Geometry defines directional bridges to:

  • Drift Dynamics

  • Collapse Geometry

  • Infrastructure Debt

  • Human Capacity Load

  • Institutional Coherence

  • Cognitive SR

  • Phenomenological SR

Each bridge requires explicit carrier and receiver‑domain evidence.

Linked concept: Directional Bridges

9. It provides SR’s strongest falsification engine

Propagation Geometry has the most explicit demotion rules in SR:

“Unsupported edges remain absent.”
“Common shock explains the synchronized pattern.”
“Path interruption does not alter receiver outcomes.”

This makes it the backbone of SR’s falsification discipline.

Linked concept: SR Falsification Protocol

10. It completes SR’s metatheory of movement

SR already had:

  • Drift (state change)

  • Collapse (viability boundary)

  • Debt (deferred obligation)

  • Human Capacity Load (compensatory work)

  • Representational Displacement (proxy drift)

Propagation Geometry adds the missing piece:

movement across the substrate.

It is the transmission pillar of the SR metatheory.

Linked concept: SR Metatheory
